After the macro, . replays the macro, as Evil's does, without Evil's 'No previous macro' error." Stock compare.vim finds 21 of them differing in text, cursor or state, and 23 with beep-aware error counts. count-percent: Evil (3,0), Vim (2,0). count-percent-keeps-column: Evil (2,3), and (1,0) without the newline because the character count shifts by one; Vim (1,0). e-stops-on-empty-line: Evil (1,0), Vim (2,2). esc-resets-goal-column: Evil (2,1), Vim (2,4). die-vim matches Evil on all of these, and none is pending. /// Whether `pos` is on the empty line after a final newline (or in an empty text). Motions never take the cursor there, but an insert session or an undo can leave it there (V1-1), and motions along that line keep it.
```rust
pub fn on_last_empty_line(t: &TextBuf, pos: usize) -> bool { pos == t.len() && t.line_start(t.line_of(pos)) == pos }
/// Where the cursor rests after an insert session or an undo: `normal_pos`, except on the empty line after a final newline, which it keeps.
pub fn rest_pos(t: &TextBuf, pos: usize) -> usize { if on_last_empty_line(t, pos) { pos } else { normal_pos(t, pos) } }
```

claim: Replaying a session for its count takes time quadratic in the count, and nothing can interrupt it. Each replayed key is its own transaction, and core lays the whole growing line out again on every edit (`normalize_views` → `snap` → `dl`). Measured: `8000ix<Esc>` takes 0.73 s in release and 1.0 s in debug, quadrupling each time the count doubles. A mistyped count of tens of thousands freezes the editor for minutes, and `99999999999999999999ix<Esc>` (which saturates to usize::MAX) never finishes.

insert.rs:130-136: `(1..s.count).try_for_each(|_| ... s.edits.iter().try_for_each(|e| apply(t, w, e)))`. Each `apply` commits a transaction, which calls `normalize_views` (text.rs:445-463). Timings from a scratch bench, `{n}ix<Esc>`:
- release: 1000 → 28 ms, 2000 → 60 ms, 4000 → 190 ms, 8000 → 732 ms
- debug: 35 ms, 76 ms, 263 ms, 1.01 s

insert::end, with three changes to the patch:
(1) Guard the fast path against empty sessions: `Some(one) if !one.is_empty() && !opens && s.count > 1 => …`. Without the guard, `3i<Esc>` inserts "", which core records as an empty undo step. With fixes.patch, `ifoo<Esc>3i<Esc>u` leaves "fooabc\n"; main gives "abc\n".
(2) Lower the cap to K4's long-line budget: `const MAX_REPEAT: usize = 1 << 20; // K4's budget is a 1 MB line; until K4's compact cells, a longer line costs ~160 bytes of layout per character.`
(3) Bound the per-key path by edit count, not size: `const MAX_REPLAY: usize = 10_000; // Each replayed edit lays the line out again until K4.` and `_ => s.edits.len().checked_mul(s.count - 1).filter(|&n| n <= MAX_REPLAY).ok_or(Error::Msg("Count too large".into())).and_then(|_| (1..s.count).try_for_each(|_| { … }))`.
For K4, record the root cause: normalize_views → snap → dl(pos) lays out the whole logical line on every commit, and set_selection lays it out twice more, so snap must cost the same whatever the line's length. Separately, core records a no-op edit (`insert(p, "")`) as an undo step. History::record should skip ops whose removed and inserted text are equal.

The patch fixes the text-only path (4,000,000 copies in 0.14 s), but the proposed fix has three problems. (a) The empty-session regression above, which I reproduced. (b) MAX_REPEAT = 64 MiB is far too high: `4000000ix<Esc>` already peaks at 650 MB RSS (measured with /usr/bin/time -l), because the whole line is laid out, so 64 MiB would need about 10 GB. (c) The per-key path stays quadratic: `4000ixy<Left><Esc>` takes 0.95 s with the patch. "Cap other replays at the same size estimate" doesn't bound time, since the cost grows with the square of the line's length, not with the bytes inserted.

claim: grammar.rs promises that the cursor never rests on a non-empty line's newline, but `e` onto a word that ends in a combining mark at the end of a line lands on the newline. `normal_pos` snaps the mark forward past its grapheme. The owner's Evil does the same (an Emacs artifact: the command loop pushes point out of a composition), and the fixture motions/combining-mark-e ("café bar" `e` → 6, the space) passes only because of that forward snap. For V3, an inclusive `de` or `ce` that took the snapped position would also delete the newline or the space.
evidence: grammar.rs:20-21 states the invariant. text.rs:164-173: `else { t.snap(p, None) }` returns `e` when `p` is inside the line's last grapheme. Evil oracle (scratch out2/deepread2.json): "café\n" (with U+0301) `e` → 6, the newline; "a café\n" `we` → 8; out/deepread.json `$` → 6. die-vim: `e` → 6, `$` → 3. So die-vim's `e` and `$` disagree on the same grapheme.
recommendation: Deviate. Evil's position here is Emacs redisplay behaviour, not Evil's grammar; Vim gives 3. Also consider whether `e` mid-line should land on "é" (3) rather than the following space (6). That would change the owner's fixture combining-mark-e, which needs the owner's sign-off, so I left it alone.

verifier.decision_view: Deviate, toward Vim, and do it uniformly: `e` lands on "é" (3) both mid-line and at the end of a line. Evil's 6 comes from Emacs's command loop pushing point out of a composition; it isn't Evil's grammar, and it is also what puts `e` on the space mid-line. The reviewer's version (snap forward mid-line, back at line end) is asymmetric and, as written, breaks repeated `e`. The deviation needs the owner's fixture combining-mark-e to change from 6 to 3. Decomposed é is rare, and the deviations review is still pending with the owner, so this is a cheap call to make now and list for veto.

claim: Escape after `f`, `F`, `t` or `T` should cancel quietly, as in Vim and in Evil, where the read quits silently. die-vim reports "f<Esc> is undefined" as an error, and, through DR-03, keeps the count for the next command.
evidence: lib.rs:59-61 binds only `f<char>` and the like. `<Esc>` isn't committed text, so the lookup falls to `Lookup::None` (ctx.rs:1230-1241). Batch Evil can't record this case: `3f<Esc>l` quit the oracle run ("After 0 kbd macro iterations: Quit"), so the test cites Vim and Evil behaviour, not a fixture.
proposed_fix: In `register`: `for key in ["f", "F", "t", "T"] { k.bind(Normal, &format!("{key}<Esc>"), "vim-cancel"); }` and `reg.command("vim-cancel", "Escape after a key that waits for another: nothing.", |_, _| Ok(()));`. Because it's a command, `run_key` takes the count even without DR-03. A18 is fine: `f` isn't bound alone. When V3 adds operators, bind `<Esc>` in OperatorPending the same way.

verifier.reasoning: On main, "abcdef\n" `3f<Esc>l` logs "f<Esc> is undefined" and leaves the cursor at 3, because the count survives (DR-03). In Evil, f reads its character with evil-read-key, and evil-read-key-map binds ESC to keyboard-quit (evil-maps.el:672). That signals quit: Emacs echoes "Quit" and clears the prefix argument, so Evil isn't fully silent, but it reports no "undefined" error. I implemented the proposed f/F/t/T<Esc> bindings to a no-op vim-cancel command; the keymap accepts them next to f<char>, and the test passes (no messages, cursor 1). The batch oracle can't record this case (quit ends the macro), as the reviewer says. `g<Esc>` stays "undefined", which matches GUI Evil, where `g <escape>` is undefined too.

claim: Suspicion, no failing test: `Vim::inserts` is never cleaned up when a buffer is killed in insert state, so one Session (with its edit list) leaks per such buffer. BufferId is a versioned slotmap key, so a leaked session can't be picked up by another buffer; the leak is only memory.
evidence: lib.rs:24 `inserts: HashMap<BufferId, Session>`. Sessions are removed only at Escape (lib.rs:174) and in `insert_edit` (lib.rs:185-188). die-vim subscribes to no kill hook.
proposed_fix: In `init`, subscribe to `on_buffer_killed` and `ctx.with_ext(|v: &mut Vim, _| v.inserts.remove(&buf))`, detached. Or do it when K5 lands the hook API.

verifier.reasoning: `Vim::inserts` (lib.rs:24) loses entries only at Escape (lib.rs:174) and in insert_edit (lib.rs:185-188), and die-vim subscribes to no kill hook. BufferId is a versioned slotmap key, so a stale entry can't be reused, and the leak is memory only, as stated. The hook doesn't have to wait for K5: `Ctx::on_buffer_killed(impl FnMut(&mut Ctx, BufferId) -> Result)` already exists (ctx.rs:983). Call it in Vim::init and `.detach()` the returned Sub; dropping the Sub cancels it (ctx.rs:232-236).
